01.note: Levi visited the house of Yosef the hunter, where he was served a peacock's head cooked in milk. He did not eat it. When he later came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi asked him why he had not excommunicated the people of that house. Levi answered that the place was the home ground of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and he thought that rabbi might have taught them to follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who allowed poultry with milk.
01.why: A teaching has just said that in Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's town people ate poultry with milk, following his view. This visit shows how the Sages treated a town that followed a local rabbi's lenient ruling.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who visited Yosef the hunter's house and refused the dish he was served.

people.name: Yosef the hunter
people.about: The host whose household served Levi a peacock's head in milk.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he asked Levi why he had not excommunicated his hosts.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: The Sage whose locale it was; Levi thought he might have ruled leniently there.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: A Sage who held that eating poultry cooked in milk is permitted.

terms.meaning: To formally shun someone from the community, a penalty the Sages could impose on those who broke their rulings.
The Torah forbids cooking a kid in its mother's milk; most Sages extended this to poultry, but Rabbi Yosei HaGelili held that birds are not included.

02.note: Rabbi Yitzhak told of a city in the Land of Israel whose people followed Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on circumcision, doing even preparatory work for it on Shabbat. Its people died at their appointed time, not before. And once, when the wicked empire, Rome, issued a decree against the Jewish people forbidding circumcision, it did not issue the decree against that city.
02.why: The mishna quoted Rabbi Eliezer allowing even trees to be cut on Shabbat to make charcoal for circumcision tools, and a teaching said his town did so. Rabbi Yitzhak's account shows that town rewarded for its devotion to the commandment.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: The Sage who tells of the city that followed Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who allowed the preparations for circumcision to be done on Shabbat.

terms.meaning: A baby boy is circumcised on his eighth day, even if it falls on Shabbat. The Sages argued over whether the preparations, like making the knife, may also be done on Shabbat.
The Land of Israel.

03.note: Rabbi Zeira had once asked Rabbi Asi a question about carrying in an alleyway, and Rabbi Asi had stayed silent. On another occasion Rabbi Zeira found him teaching a report: once people forgot to bring the circumcision knife before Shabbat and brought it on Shabbat, and the Rabbis were troubled that Rabbi Eliezer's view had been followed. Rabbi Oshaya added that the circumciser told him it was carried only from one end of an unmerged alleyway to the other. Rabbi Zeira asked whether Rabbi Asi now held that carrying there was allowed; he said yes. Asked why he had not said so before, he agreed that his knowledge had come back to him in the course of his studies.
03.why: Rabbi Zeira's earlier question, whether one may carry throughout an alleyway whose residents never merged, went unanswered. This later scene supplies Rabbi Asi's answer, which the Gemara then compares with Rav's ruling that such an alleyway allows carrying only four cubits.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who had asked Rabbi Asi a question earlier and found him teaching the answer later.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage who could not answer Rabbi Zeira at first, then later taught a case that answered it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: The Sage in whose name the report of the forgotten knife is told.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: A Sage who asked the circumciser where the knife was carried.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda the Cutter
people.about: A circumciser who told Rabbi Oshaya the knife was carried within an alleyway.

terms.meaning: Residents of courtyards opening onto a shared alleyway can pool food in a joint arrangement that lets them carry there on Shabbat. Here they had not done so.
A follower of the School of Shammai, whose views the law usually does not follow.
A rule that when one Sage disagrees with the majority, the law follows the majority.

04.note: When Rava taught the public in Mehoza how to make a bandage, the sons of Manyomei the doctor tore their clothes, since everyone could now treat themselves. Rava told them he had left them one cure to profit from: Shmuel said that one who washes his face and does not dry it well will get sores, and the remedy is to wash a great deal in water in which beets have been boiled.
04.why: The mishna allows a bandage on a circumcision wound on Shabbat, and Rava has just given the recipe for a bandage, wax and tree sap. This story tells what happened when he taught that recipe in public.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who taught a bandage recipe in Mehoza.

people.name: Manyomei the doctor
people.about: A doctor whose sons were upset that Rava gave away a cure.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose teaching about face sores Rava passed on to the doctor's sons.

terms.meaning: A traditional sign of grief or distress.

05.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar told how Rabbi Meir once had stomach pain on Shabbat, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and those with him wanted to mix wine and oil for him. He would not let them. They asked whether his own ruling would be cancelled in his lifetime. He answered that although he held his view and his colleagues held theirs, he had never in his life dared to go against his colleagues' words. The Gemara concludes that he was strict only with himself.
05.why: A teaching cites Rabbi Meir as allowing wine and oil to be mixed for a sick person on Shabbat. This incident seems to show him refusing it, and the Gemara reads it so that the permission still stands for everyone else.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: The Sage who tells the story; he was among those who wanted to treat Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who allowed mixing wine and oil for the sick but refused it for himself.

terms.meaning: A remedy for the sick. The Sages forbade preparing medicines on Shabbat, and argued over whether this mixture counts.

06.note: Rabbi Natan told how, on a visit to the coastal cities, a woman came to him who had circumcised her first son and he died, and her second son and he died. She brought her third son to him. He saw the baby was red and told her to wait until the blood was absorbed into him. She waited, then circumcised him, and he lived. People called the boy Natan the Babylonian, after him.
06.why: Abaye has just quoted his foster mother: a baby who is red has not yet absorbed his blood, so his circumcision should wait. Rabbi Natan's account is brought as the source for that advice.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage, called the Babylonian, who advised a mother to delay her son's circumcision.

people.name: Natan the Babylonian
people.about: The name given to the baby who lived, after Rabbi Natan.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the era of the Mishna that was not included in the Mishna itself.

07.note: Rabbi Natan told of a second visit, to Cappadocia. Again a woman whose first two sons had died after circumcision brought her third son to him. He saw that the baby was pale and could find in him no blood of the covenant. He told her to wait until blood came into him. She waited, circumcised him, and he lived, and he too was called Natan the Babylonian after him.
07.why: Abaye has quoted his foster mother that a pale baby should not be circumcised until his blood comes into him. This second account of Rabbi Natan's supports that half of her advice, as the first account supported the advice about a red baby.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who advised a mother in Cappadocia to delay circumcising her pale baby.

people.name: Natan the Babylonian
people.about: The name given to the baby who lived, after Rabbi Natan.

terms.meaning: The blood drawn at circumcision, which is called the covenant between God and Abraham's descendants.

08.note: A man came before Rava with a question about washing a newly circumcised baby, and Rava gave him the ruling he himself held. Afterward Rava fell ill and said: Why did I set myself against the views of the Elders? The Sages said to him that a teaching supported his view. He answered that the wording of the mishna fits theirs.
08.why: The Gemara has a baraita that matches Rava's reading of the mishna on when a circumcised baby may be washed on Shabbat. The story shows Rava himself backing away from it in favor of the Elders' stricter reading.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who ruled on washing a baby, fell ill, and regretted contradicting the Elders.

terms.meaning: Earlier Sages whose ruling on washing a baby was stricter than Rava's. The translation names them as Rav Yehuda and Rabba bar Avuh.
The core legal text of rabbinic law, compiled around 200 CE, on which the Gemara comments.

09.note: A son was born to Rav Adda bar Ahava already circumcised. He went around to thirteen circumcisers, and in the end the child was left with a severed urethra. Rav Adda said: I deserved this, because I went against Rav's ruling. Rav Nahman asked him: And did you not go against Shmuel's too? Shmuel required drawing a drop of blood only on a weekday, not on Shabbat. The Gemara explains that Rav Adda held such a child certainly has a hidden foreskin.
09.why: The Gemara has just stated a dispute: Rav said a baby born circumcised needs nothing done, while Shmuel said a drop of covenant blood must be drawn. Rav Adda's son shows what came of acting against Rav, and Rav Nahman's question turns to whether this may be done on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage whose son was born circumcised and was injured when the boy was circumcised.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who ruled that a baby born circumcised needs no further cutting.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who required drawing a drop of blood from a baby born circumcised.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who asked Rav Adda whether he had gone against Shmuel too.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who held there is only a doubt that such a baby has a hidden foreskin.

terms.meaning: A baby born without a visible foreskin. The Sages debated whether a drop of blood must still be drawn as a sign of the covenant.
A foreskin present but hidden under the skin, which would mean the baby still needs a real circumcision.
An injury to the urinary passage, here caused by a botched circumcision.

10.note: A baby born to the son of Rav Dimi bar Yosef died within thirty days of birth, and the father sat in mourning for him. His own father, Rav Dimi bar Yosef, asked him whether he only wanted the special foods given to mourners. The son answered that he was certain the baby had been carried to full term.
10.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a baby who dies within thirty days counts as having been born viable, as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel held. This father explains why he mourns anyway: he knew the pregnancy was full term.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who questioned his son for mourning a baby who died within thirty days.

people.name: son of Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: A father who mourned his baby and said he knew the child was full term.

terms.meaning: A baby who dies before thirty days may be treated as never having been viable, so the usual mourning rites need not apply.
Mourners are served a meal by others. Rav Dimi suggests his son mourns only to get it.

11.note: Rav Ashi visited the house of Rav Kahana, whose child died within thirty days of birth. Rav Ashi saw Rav Kahana sitting in mourning for him and asked whether he did not follow Shmuel's ruling, as reported by Rav Yehuda, that the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rav Kahana answered that he was certain the child had been carried to full term.
11.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a baby who dies within thirty days counts as viable. This second account of a parent mourning such a baby gives the same answer as the one before it: a full-term birth is treated differently.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who visited Rav Kahana and questioned his mourning.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage whose baby died within thirty days and who mourned him.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who ruled that the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: A Sage who held that a baby who has not lived thirty days may be treated as never viable.

terms.meaning: A baby who dies before thirty days may be treated as never having been viable, so the usual mourning rites need not apply.

12.note: The people of Bashkar sent three questions to Levi: may a canopy be spread on Shabbat, are hops in a vineyard a forbidden mixture of crops, and what is done when someone dies on a Festival. While the messenger was on the way, Levi died. Shmuel told Rav Menashya to answer them if he was wise enough. Rav Menashya wrote that they had examined every side of the canopy question and found no way to permit it.
12.why: The Gemara returns to the law of a canopy on Shabbat. Afterward it asks why Rav Menashya hid the lenient views that existed, and answers that the people of Bashkar were not learned enough to apply them safely.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage to whom the people of Bashkar sent questions; he died before they arrived.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who told Rav Menashya to answer the questions.

people.name: Rav Menashya
people.about: The Sage who sent answers to the people of Bashkar.

terms.meaning: A tent-like covering over a bed. Spreading one on Shabbat can count as building a tent, which is forbidden.
The Torah forbids sowing other crops in a vineyard; the question was whether hops count.
A biblical holy day, such as Passover, on which most work is forbidden, as on Shabbat.

13.note: Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheilat reported in Rabbi Asi's name an incident in the synagogue of Maon on a Festival next to Shabbat. Someone died; he did not know whether the Festival fell before Shabbat or after it. They came before Rabbi Yohanan, who told them to let gentiles attend to the burial.
13.why: Rav Menashya had told the people of Bashkar that neither Jews nor gentiles may bury a body on a Festival. The Gemara cites this ruling of Rabbi Yohanan to challenge him, then explains he was strict because they were not learned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheilat
people.about: A Sage who passed on the report in Rabbi Asi's name.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: The Sage who told of the incident at Maon.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who ruled that gentiles may bury the dead person on the Festival.

terms.meaning: A holy day falling on the day before or after Shabbat, so that two days of rest run together and burial would be put off.
A biblical holy day on which most work is forbidden.

14.note: Rav Yosef said that once he followed Mar Ukva into a bathhouse. When he came out, Mar Ukva gave him one cup of this wine drink, and he felt its chill from the hair on his head to the nails of his feet. Had he been given a second cup, he said, he would have feared that it would use up his reward in the World to Come. The Gemara asks how Mar Ukva drank it every day, and answers that he was used to it.
14.why: A teaching has just said that aluntit, a drink of aged wine, water and balsam taken after the bathhouse, may not be prepared on Shabbat because it is a remedy. Rav Yosef's experience shows how strong a drink it was.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who tasted the cooling bathhouse drink.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who gave Rav Yosef the drink and took it himself every day.

terms.meaning: The reward of the righteous after this life. Rav Yosef feared a second cup of pleasure would be paid out of it.
A drink of aged wine, clear water and balsam, taken to cool down after the bathhouse.

15.note: Rav Aha bar Yosef had heaviness of the heart. Mar Ukva told him to drink asafoetida over three days. He drank on Thursday and Friday, then on Shabbat morning asked in the study hall what to do. They told him a person may drink it on Shabbat without concern. He said his question was about soaking it, not drinking it. Rav Hiyya bar Avin said the same thing had happened to him: Rav Adda bar Ahava had no answer, and Rav Huna said that Rav's view was to soak it in cold water and set it in the sun.
15.why: The Gemara has just reported Rabbi Yannai ruling that soaking asafoetida even in cold water is forbidden. This case of a patient mid-treatment brings Rav's lenient ruling, which the Gemara then says could hold even for Rabbi Yannai, because stopping would endanger him.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage with heaviness of the heart who asked about preparing his remedy on Shabbat.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who prescribed the asafoetida treatment.

people.name: Rav Hiyya bar Avin
people.about: A Sage who had faced the same question and reported the answer.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage who could not answer Rav Hiyya bar Avin's question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who answered in Rav's name: soak it in cold water and set it in the sun.

terms.meaning: A strong-smelling plant resin, soaked in water and drunk as a remedy.
An ailment felt as pain or pressure in the chest.
A measure of volume, a few liters.
The place where the Sages and their students learned together and answered questions.

16.note: Rav Hisda held a pearl in one hand and a clod of earth in the other while teaching his daughters. He showed them the pearl straight away. The clod he did not show them until they grew upset with curiosity, and only then did he show it.
16.why: Rav Hisda has been advising his daughters to be modest before their husbands. The Gemara presents this demonstration as his lesson in that modesty, in which what is hidden draws more interest than what is on display.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who gave advice to his daughters and showed them a pearl and a clod of earth.

17.note: Abaye would put a spoon on bundles of produce so he could move them on Shabbat, and Rava would put a knife on a slaughtered young dove and move it. Rav Yosef mocked them: how sharp is the law of children! The Sages allowed this only for someone who forgot, not to be planned in advance. Abaye answered that the bundles could anyway be leaned on, and he used the spoon only because he was an important person. Rava said the same: the dove was fit to eat raw, so the knife was needed only because he was an important person.
17.why: The Gemara has quoted rulings that a forgotten object may be moved on Shabbat by setting bread or a baby on it, and Rav Ashi limited this. These Sages using the trick on purpose bring the question of when it is allowed.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who put a spoon on bundles of produce to move them on Shabbat.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who put a knife on a slaughtered young dove to move it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who mocked their practice as the law of children.

terms.meaning: From the outset, as a planned first choice, as against a fix after the fact.
A respected Sage, expected to be stricter in public so that others do not learn the wrong lesson from him.

18.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi sat before Rabbi Yohanan while he dozed. Rabbi Hiyya asked a string of questions: why are the birds of Babylonia fat, its Festivals joyous, its Torah scholars marked by their dress, and gentiles contaminated? Rabbi Asi had a quick answer for each. Rabbi Yohanan woke and scolded them: children, only say what is as clear to you as the fact that your sister is forbidden to you. When they asked him to answer, he said the birds of Babylonia are fat because they were never exiled, as a verse about Moab shows.
18.why: The mishna mentioned the kolyas, a fish from Spain, and Rabbi Abba's chicken from the Land of Israel, and the Gemara has been comparing Babylonian and Israeli food and tastes. This exchange turns to the differences between the two lands.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: A Sage who asked questions about Babylonia while Rabbi Yohanan dozed.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage who gave quick answers to Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba's questions.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Their teacher, who woke, rebuked their guessing, and began to answer himself.

terms.term: Say to wisdom: You are my sister
terms.meaning: A verse from Proverbs, read by Rabbi Yohanan to mean that one should teach only what one knows as surely as one knows a sister is forbidden in marriage.
The land in what is now Iraq, home to a large Jewish community and its own academies of Sages.

18.flag: The STORY ends after Rabbi Yohanan's first answer; his answers to the remaining questions continue in the AFTER segments, so the scene is cut off midway.

19.note: Ulla came to Pumbedita and saw the rabbis there shaking dust from their cloaks on Shabbat. He said: The Rabbis are desecrating Shabbat. Rav Yehuda told the rabbis to go on shaking their cloaks in front of him, because in their place people were not at all particular about this.
19.why: Rav Huna has just ruled that shaking dust from a cloak on Shabbat counts as laundering, but only for new black garments whose owner is particular about them. This story shows the last condition in practice.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage who objected to the rabbis of Pumbedita shaking their cloaks.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who told the rabbis they could keep shaking their cloaks in Ulla's presence.

terms.meaning: Doing work forbidden on the Sabbath.
Caring about keeping a garment clean. The Gemara rules that shaking off dust is forbidden only for someone who does care.

20.note: Abaye was standing before Rav Yosef, who asked him for his hat. Abaye saw there was dew on it and hesitated to hand it over. Rav Yosef told him to shake it off and throw it to him, since they were not at all particular about this.
20.why: Rav Huna has ruled that shaking a garment on Shabbat counts as laundering only if the owner is particular about keeping it clean. Like the story of Ulla in Pumbedita before it, this one shows that rule in practice.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A student who hesitated to hand Rav Yosef a hat with dew on it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who told him to shake off the dew and throw him the hat.

terms.meaning: Caring about keeping a garment clean. Shaking off dust or dew on Shabbat is forbidden only for someone who does care.
